idiom_name: each with a block, plus the Enumerable messages (map/select/reject/inject/find)
implementation_notes: Ruby keeps Beck's original shape almost literally: the enumeration message is each and the action is a block, so a class becomes enumerable by defining each and including Enumerable, which then supplies the collect/select/reject/inject/detect family (map, select, reject, inject/reduce, find) - the same message vocabulary the Smalltalk catalogue names. each_with_index, each_with_object and zip supply position or accumulator state when a plain index loop would have been used, and lazy/Enumerator variants add the lazy walk. The block form stays the right choice for side-effecting walks; the transforming messages win as soon as a result is wanted, because hand-building the result collection is the code the pattern removes.
code_sketch:
order.lines.each { |line| apply_discount(line, policy) }   # block = the action

class Order
  include Enumerable
  def each(&block) = @lines.each(&block)      # one message, storage hidden
end

total = order.lines.select(&:taxable?).sum(&:amount)   # Enumerable messages
pitfalls: Mutating the receiver inside each (delete/insert) skips or repeats elements; collect the changes and apply them after the walk.
Blocks and lambdas differ in arity and return semantics: break/next inside a block flow differently, and return inside a block returns from the enclosing method, not just the block.
each returns the receiver, not a mapped result - chains that should have used map silently continue with the original collection.
